warmup.q: A Kotlin class gives Java a door: fun cookAsync(order: Order): CompletableFuture<Outcome> = scope.future { cook(order) }. A Java caller adds .orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS), and the timeout fires. What happens to the Kotlin coroutine?
options: Nothing: a Java timeout can't reach a Kotlin coroutine
It is cancelled, because the future it belongs to completed
It keeps running, and its result is ignored when it arrives
The JVM interrupts the thread the coroutine runs on
warmup.why: The future returned by future { } is tied to its coroutine: the KDoc says the coroutine is cancelled when the future "is cancelled or otherwise completed". orTimeout completes that same future exceptionally, so the coroutine is cancelled at its next suspension point. Nothing is interrupted, and nothing keeps running.

opening:
Next door lives a neighbour who cooks the old way. Ask her for a pie, and she hands you a ticket: "Come back with this, and the pie will be ready." Our kitchen runs on bookmarks and timers, hers on tickets, and each works fine on its own. The trouble is at the fence. If our cook stands at the neighbour's door holding the ticket, every pot in our kitchen waits with her. And if the guests call dinner off, nobody tells the neighbour, and she bakes a pie that nobody will eat.

In code, the neighbour is Java. A CompletableFuture is her ticket, and she may also cook with Reactor or with virtual threads. Shared state and testing coroutines stayed inside Kotlin, but real programs mix both. The easy trap is to cross the fence with whatever works in a demo, a blocking get() or a runBlocking, and lose the cancel on the way.

In this lesson, we'll cross the fence both ways with futures, then with Reactor, give Java code a door it can use, and weigh the three ways of cooking against each other. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the fence between two kitchens, with the neighbour's ticket and a cook who mustn't stand at her door. await() waits for a Java future without holding a thread and passes the cancel across. future { } and mono { } hand Java and Reactor tickets tied to the coroutine, and each of the three ways of cooking suits a different kitchen.

Now search your own code for .get() or .join() on a future inside a coroutine, and for runBlocking inside supplyAsync. Each one is a cook standing at the neighbour's door.

That ends this track. Next, in Kotlin Flow in depth, we'll take the recipe card apart. What is a Flow made of, underneath map and collect?

sections.h: Cross the fence with futures: await() in, future { } out
sections.html:
Most Java code that waits for something speaks CompletableFuture. A future is an object that stands for a result that isn't ready yet: the neighbour's ticket. kotlinx.coroutines crosses the fence in both directions with nothing extra to add to the build, since the old kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8 artifact was merged into the core library in 1.7.

Start with the way in. The bakery has a Java library whose loavesLeft(bread) returns a future at once, and the future completes later with the number of loaves left. Here is the naive bridge, which the lab's starting code uses, and the fixed one:

Java
// Java equivalent: block a thread on the future, or chain on it
int loaves = bakery.loavesLeft("rye").join();                                       // blocks the caller
CompletableFuture<String> note = bakery.loavesLeft("rye").thenApply(n -> n + " left");   // or composes
Kotlin
// Naive: an IO thread stands at the door for the whole wait, and a cancel never reaches the future
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { bakery.loavesLeft("rye").get() }

// Fixed: suspends until the future completes; cancelling this coroutine cancels the future
bakery.loavesLeft("rye").await()

The naive version "doesn't block the caller", and that's why it ships. But get() blocks an IO thread for the whole wait, the cook standing at the neighbour's door. Worse, if the calling coroutine is cancelled, the future never hears about it.

await() suspends instead, so no thread waits. It rethrows the future's exception unwrapped, so you catch the IOException itself rather than an ExecutionException, and it has a fast path for a future that is already done. It also carries the cancel across: if the awaiting coroutine is cancelled, await() calls future.cancel(false). That is usually right, because nobody wants the answer any more. When the future is shared, or must finish anyway (a pie already in the oven), use future.asDeferred().await(), which waits without cancelling it.

Now the way out. Our kitchen can hand the neighbour a ticket too:

Java
// Java equivalent: the Java caller's side, which is plain CompletableFuture code
CompletableFuture<String> reply = door.cookAsync(new Order("soup", 4))
    .orTimeout(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .thenApply(outcome -> "soup: " + outcome);
Kotlin
class KitchenDoor(private val cook: suspend (Order) -> Outcome) : AutoCloseable {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)

    fun cookAsync(order: Order): CompletableFuture<Outcome> = scope.future { cook(order) }

    override fun close() = scope.cancel()
}

future { } is a builder like async: it starts a coroutine in the scope and hands its result back as a CompletableFuture. The link runs both ways. The KDoc, the documentation in the library's source, says the coroutine is cancelled when the future "is cancelled or otherwise completed". So a Java caller's cancel(true), or an orTimeout that fires, cancels the Kotlin coroutine. Give the door a scope it owns, as in Structured concurrency, so that closing the door cancels everything still cooking. GlobalScope.future also compiles, and it leaks in exactly the way that lesson described.

Predict three lines before you run FutureBridge, in the Try it below:

1. await() on a Java future, then cancel the coroutine:
  future cancelled: true
2. asDeferred().await(), then cancel the coroutine:
  future cancelled: false  (it still completes: apple pie ready)
3. future { } for a Java caller, who cancels it:
  [kotlin] cooking leek was cancelled
  future cancelled: true

The cancel crossed the fence both ways. In case 1, cancelling the coroutine cancelled the neighbour's future. In case 3, the Java caller cancelled the future, and the Kotlin coroutine heard it at its next suspension point. Here the picture breaks a little. Cancelling a plain Java future only marks it as cancelled. Whether the work behind it stops depends on the code that made it, just as a real neighbour may or may not read your note. A future from future { } always stops its coroutine.

Cross the fence with await() and future { }. get() and runBlocking hold a thread and drop the cancel.

The neighbour across the road cooks another way again, with Reactor.

try.title: Cancel across the fence
steps: Read FutureBridge.kt. Predict the three future cancelled lines.
Run the Java twin. It is plain Java calling the Kotlin SoupKitchen from the same file, so watch for the [kotlin] lines.
In the Java twin, change orTimeout(50, ...) to orTimeout(500, ...) and run it again. Predict first.

code.title: FutureBridge.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.future.asDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.future.await import kotlinx.coroutines.future.future import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Kotlin code with a face for Java: the suspend call gets a CompletableFuture twin. */ class SoupKitchen : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) /** Cooks a pot of [soup] and returns how many bowls it made. */ suspend fun cook(soup: String): Int { try { delay(200) // simmering return soup.length * 7 } catch (e: kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException) { println(" [kotlin] cooking $soup was cancelled") throw e } } fun cookAsync(soup: String): CompletableFuture<Int> = scope.future { cook(soup) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } /** The neighbour's Java-style future: a pie that takes 500 ms. It reports whether someone cancelled it. */ fun neighboursPie(): CompletableFuture<String> { val f = CompletableFuture<String>() CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).execute { f.complete("apple pie ready") } return f } fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. await() on a Java future, then cancel the coroutine:") val f1 = neighboursPie() launch { f1.await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f1.isCancelled}") println("2. asDeferred().await(), then cancel the coroutine:") val f2 = neighboursPie() launch { f2.asDeferred().await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f2.isCancelled} (it still completes: ${f2.get()})") println("3. future { } for a Java caller, who cancels it:") SoupKitchen().use { kitchen -> val f3 = kitchen.cookAsync("leek") delay(50) f3.cancel(true) delay(50) println(" future cancelled: ${f3.isCancelled}") } }

alt.title: FutureBridgeJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FutureBridge.kt, from the Java side: plain Java calling the Kotlin // SoupKitchen through its future {} method. No Continuation, no runBlocking. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class FutureBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (SoupKitchen kitchen = new SoupKitchen()) { System.out.println("1. compose two Kotlin calls like any futures:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> bowls = kitchen.cookAsync("leek") .thenCombine(kitchen.cookAsync("tomato"), Integer::sum); System.out.println(" bowls in total: " + bowls.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); System.out.println("2. a Java timeout cancels the Kotlin coroutine:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> slow = kitchen.cookAsync("onion") .orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // fails the future after 50 ms try { slow.join(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" java caller got: " + e.getCause()); } Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("3. cancel(true) on the future the kitchen returned:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> cancelled = kitchen.cookAsync("pea"); Thread.sleep(50); cancelled.cancel(true); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println(" future cancelled: " + cancelled.isCancelled()); } } }

try.expect: Case 1 prints future cancelled: true: cancelling the coroutine cancelled the Java future it was awaiting. Case 2 prints false, and the future still completes, because asDeferred().await() only waits. Case 3 prints [kotlin] cooking leek was cancelled, then true. In the Java twin, the two soups make 70 bowls between them, and both the orTimeout and the cancel(true) produce a [kotlin] ... was cancelled line. With a 500 ms timeout the 200 ms soup finishes first, so there is no timeout and no cancel line for it.

sections.h: Cross into Reactor: mono { } out, awaitSingle() and asFlow() in
sections.html:
Reactor, the subject of the reactive track, is a Java library for streams of values. A Mono is a recipe for at most one value, a Flux is a recipe for many, and nothing runs until someone subscribes. The kotlinx-coroutines-reactor module, on this lab's classpath, bridges both:

Java
// Java equivalent: the Reactor side just sees ordinary Mono and Flux values
Mono<Recipe> soup = RecipeMonoKt.recipeMono(book, "soup");             // built by mono { } in Kotlin
Mono<String> both = Mono.zip(soup, RecipeMonoKt.recipeMono(book, "bread")).map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2());
Flux<Integer> temps = ReactorBridgeKt.temperatureFlux();                // a Kotlin Flow through asFlux()
Kotlin
fun recipeMono(book: RecipeBook, dish: String): Mono<Recipe> = mono { book.recipe(dish) }   // suspend code as a Mono
suspend fun recipeNow(dish: String): Recipe = recipeFromReactor(dish).awaitSingle()      // a Mono in suspend code
fun plates(): Flow<String> = plateFlux().asFlow()                                         // a Flux as a Flow
fun temperatureFlux(): Flux<Int> = temperatures().asFlux()                                // a Flow as a Flux

mono { } gives a cold Mono: the coroutine starts on subscription, once per subscriber, which is the contract every Reactor user expects (Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe). It's the recipe card of Flow basics again: each subscriber cooks from it afresh. A null result completes the Mono empty, and disposing the subscription cancels the coroutine. Its context may not contain a Job ("Mono context cannot contain job in it"), because the subscription owns the coroutine's life, not a scope. flux { } does the same for a stream of values, with send inside.

In the other direction, awaitSingle() waits for exactly one value, and throws NoSuchElementException for an empty Mono; awaitSingleOrNull() returns null instead. Publisher.asFlow() collects a Flux as a Flow. The Flow's suspension becomes request(n), the Reactive Streams call by which a subscriber asks for n more values, and cancelling the collector cancels the subscription. Flow.asFlux() goes back. The module's README calls the result TCK-compliant: it passes the Reactive Streams test kit (TCK), which checks a publisher against the numbered rules of the specification.

ReactorBridge, in the Try it below, looks up a recipe twice through one Mono, then asks for a dish the book doesn't have:

1. mono { } is cold:
  built the Mono; nothing looked up yet
  [kotlin] looking up soup
  awaitSingle() -> soup: 40 minutes
  [kotlin] looking up soup
  awaitSingle() again -> soup: 40 minutes
2. an empty Mono:
  [kotlin] looking up dragon stew
  awaitSingle() threw NoSuchElementException

Building the Mono looked up nothing. Each awaitSingle() subscribed, and each subscription ran the coroutine again. The recipe book, sensibly, has nothing for dragon stew, so that Mono completed empty, and awaitSingle() threw. If one lookup must be shared, .cache() on the Mono does it.

Two things need care. Threads first: unless you pass a dispatcher, mono { } starts its coroutine on Dispatchers.Default, while the Reactor operators around it run wherever their schedulers put them. Then context: Reactor's own Context, which a Reactor-based web framework uses for values such as a request id, is visible inside the coroutine as a ReactorContext element. Thread-local values are not, for the reason Dispatchers and the coroutine context gave: a coroutine may resume on another thread.

mono { } runs its coroutine once per subscriber, and disposing the subscription cancels it.

Futures and Monos are shapes Java code already knows. Plain Java can call our suspend functions too, if we give it a door.

steps: Read ReactorBridge.kt. Predict how many [kotlin] looking up soup lines print in part 1.
Run the Java twin, which uses the same Kotlin recipeFor and temperatureFlux functions from plain Reactor code.
In the Kotlin file, change awaitSingle() in part 2 to awaitSingleOrNull() and print the result. Predict first.

code.title: ReactorBridge.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.asFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.awaitSingle import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.asFlux import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.mono import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration /** A Kotlin suspend call, handed to Reactor code as a cold Mono. */ fun recipeFor(dish: String): Mono<String> = mono { println(" [kotlin] looking up $dish") delay(50) if (dish == "dragon stew") null else "$dish: 40 minutes" } /** A Kotlin Flow of oven temperatures, handed to Reactor code as a Flux. */ fun temperatures(): Flow<Int> = flow { for (i in 0 until 5) { delay(20); emit(180 + i * 5) } } fun temperatureFlux(): Flux<Int> = temperatures().asFlux() fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. mono { } is cold:") val m = recipeFor("soup") println(" built the Mono; nothing looked up yet") println(" awaitSingle() -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println(" awaitSingle() again -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println("2. an empty Mono:") try { recipeFor("dragon stew").awaitSingle() } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println(" awaitSingle() threw NoSuchElementException") } println("3. a Flux consumed as a Flow (cancelling the flow cancels the subscription):") val plates = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(10)).map { "plate-$it" }.doOnCancel { println(" [reactor] subscription cancelled") } println(" ${plates.asFlow().take(3).toList()}") println("4. a Flow handed to Reactor as a Flux:") println(" ${temperatureFlux().map { "$it C" }.collectList().block()}") }

alt.title: ReactorBridgeJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ReactorBridge.kt, from the Java side: Reactor code using the Kotlin // functions through their Mono and Flux faces. The Kotlin side is ReactorBridge.kt. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ReactorBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. the Kotlin Mono is cold, so each subscription looks it up again:"); Mono<String> soup = ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("soup"); System.out.println(" built the Mono; nothing looked up yet"); System.out.println(" block() -> " + soup.block()); System.out.println(" block() again -> " + soup.block()); System.out.println("2. an empty Mono and a default:"); System.out.println(" " + ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("dragon stew").defaultIfEmpty("no recipe: make toast").block()); System.out.println("3. zip two Kotlin lookups with Reactor operators:"); System.out.println(" " + Mono.zip(ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("soup"), ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("bread")) .map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2()).block()); System.out.println("4. a Kotlin Flow as a Flux:"); List<String> temps = ReactorBridgeKt.temperatureFlux().map(c -> c + " C").collectList().block(); System.out.println(" " + temps); } }

try.expect: [kotlin] looking up soup prints twice in part 1, once per awaitSingle(), and not when the Mono is built: mono { } is cold. Part 2 throws NoSuchElementException for the empty Mono, and after your change it prints null. Part 3 prints three plates and [reactor] subscription cancelled, because take(3) stopped the Flow. Part 4 prints five temperatures from 180 C to 200 C. The Java twin shows the same cold Mono from the Reactor side, plus defaultIfEmpty and Mono.zip over two Kotlin lookups.

sections.h: Give Java callers a door they can use
sections.html:
Java can see a suspend function, but it can't call it in any useful way. The compiler adds a Continuation parameter, the bookmark of Suspend functions from zero, and changes the return type to Object. So from Java the signature looks like this:

Java
// what Java sees for the same function: a Continuation parameter and an Object result
public Object cook(Order order, Continuation<? super Outcome> $completion)
Kotlin
suspend fun cook(order: Order): Outcome

You could write a Continuation by hand, but you'd be rebuilding a coroutine builder, badly. Give Java callers one of three doors instead.

  • A CompletableFuture door, built with future { }, like the lab's KitchenDoor. It's the default for Java code that composes its work as futures.
  • A Mono door, built with mono { }, for code that already lives in Reactor.
  • A blocking door that wraps runBlocking { }, for Java callers that block anyway: a command-line tool, a JUnit test, or any code running on a virtual thread. Blocking a virtual thread is cheap, so runBlocking on one is a fair bridge. It's still wrong inside suspend code, as Builders showed.

Whichever you choose, name the doors so the difference shows: cook for Kotlin, cookAsync or cookBlocking for Java. Keep the suspend function as the one real implementation, and make the others thin wrappers, so the rules for retries and timeouts live in one place. @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic and @JvmName take care of the rest of what Java sees: default arguments, functions in a companion object, and names that would clash.

A blocking door needs a timeout of its own. runBlocking { withTimeout(2.seconds) { cook(order) } } gives the Java caller an upper bound. And an interrupt of the calling thread, Java's request to stop from the first track, cancels the coroutine and makes runBlocking throw InterruptedException. That's the bridge from Java's way of cancelling to Kotlin's.

The lab's Java test, JavaCallerTest.java, shows what a Java caller ends up writing against a future { } door: orTimeout, thenApply and get, with no Kotlin types in sight beyond the data classes.

Quick check: two Java callers wait for the kitchen through different doors, and each caller's thread is interrupted while the dish is cooking. Caller A uses cookBlocking, the runBlocking door. Caller B calls cookAsync(order).get(). Whose cooking is cancelled? (Only A's. The interrupt reaches runBlocking, which cancels its coroutine. B's interrupt only makes get() throw InterruptedException. The future isn't complete, so the coroutine behind it keeps cooking until someone cancels the future or closes the door.)

Keep one suspend function as the real code, and give Java thin doors: a future, a Mono, or a blocking call with its own timeout.

Three neighbours, three ways of cooking. Which one should a new program start with?

sections.h: Virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor: choosing for a new program
sections.html:
All three solve the problem the virtual threads track opened with. A program that answers many requests at once spends most of its time waiting, for a database or for another web service, and an operating-system thread per waiting request is too expensive. They solve it at different layers. Virtual threads, final since JDK 21, are threads so cheap that a waiting one costs almost nothing: a helper at every pot, who simply stands there. Coroutines make waiting explicit with suspend, and add a tree of dishes with cancellation and Flow. Reactor turns a request into a line of stations, with backpressure: a slow consumer slows down a fast producer.

ThreeWays, in the Try it below, cooks the same dinner each way: soup in 100 ms, the roast in 300 and the salad in 200, all started at once. Predict the times:

coroutines:                       [soup, roast, salad]
  took 304 ms on main
blocking code on virtual threads: [soup, roast, salad]
  took 332 ms
blocking code on Dispatchers.IO: [soup, roast, salad]
  took 318 ms

Each one takes as long as the slowest dish, and the Java twin's virtual threads and Reactor Mono.zip did the same (309 and 301 ms). Speed doesn't decide between them. The shape of your code does:

Virtual threads (JDK 21+) Kotlin coroutines Reactor
Picture it a cheap helper standing at every pot one cook, bookmarks and a tree of dishes a line of stations
Your code looks like plain blocking Java or Kotlin sequential suspend functions chains of operators
Blocking libraries (database drivers, older SDKs) the natural fit withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher wrap them, move them to boundedElastic
Several calls with one deadline StructuredTaskScope, preview in JDK 25 coroutineScope, async, withTimeout Mono.zip, timeout
Cancellation interrupts, if the code checks them flows down the job tree to every child a cancel signal up the chain
Streams with backpressure none built in Flow Flux
Debugging ordinary stacks and thread dumps debug mode and coroutine dumps operator traces, harder to read
Java callers native through future { } or mono { } native

Here is what I would do in a program that answers many requests and talks to a database through a blocking driver.

  • Start with virtual threads for request handling that is mostly blocking calls. Database drivers and many older libraries block anyway. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized no longer pins a virtual thread to its carrier, the platform thread that runs it, in most cases, so JDK 25 is a good base. Cap each slow neighbour with a semaphore, a counter of permits, as Using virtual threads showed.
  • Use coroutines in Kotlin code that needs what virtual threads don't give you: several calls with one deadline, a cancel that reaches every child, Flow pipelines, StateFlow-style shared state. Blocking calls inside still go through withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher.
  • Keep Reactor where a reactive stack already exists, or where you stream with backpressure from end to end. Don't start a new program full of blocking calls on it.

Mixing them is normal, and cheap with the bridges from this lesson. What to avoid is several models in one call path for no reason: a coroutine that calls runBlocking, which subscribes to a Mono, which blocks on a database. That's three kitchens to boil one egg, and a cancel has to cross every fence on the way.

Pick one model for each part of the program, and convert only at its edges.

Whichever you pick, the bridges in this lesson keep a cancel from getting lost at the fence.

In ThreeWays.kt, wrap the body of dinnerWithCoroutines in withTimeout(250) { ... } and run it again. What happens to the dishes still cooking?

code.title: ThreeWays.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis // one dinner: soup (100 ms), roast (300 ms) and salad (200 ms), all started at once suspend fun dinnerWithCoroutines(): List<String> = coroutineScope { val soup = async { delay(100); "soup" } val roast = async { delay(300); "roast" } val salad = async { delay(200); "salad" } listOf(soup.await(), roast.await(), salad.await()) } /** The same dinner written as BLOCKING code, run on whatever dispatcher you pass. */ suspend fun dinnerBlocking(on: CoroutineDispatcher): List<String> = coroutineScope { val soup = async(on) { Thread.sleep(100); "soup" } val roast = async(on) { Thread.sleep(300); "roast" } val salad = async(on) { Thread.sleep(200); "salad" } listOf(soup.await(), roast.await(), salad.await()) } fun main() = runBlocking { repeat(2) { dinnerWithCoroutines() } // warm up val c = measureTimeMillis { println("coroutines: ${dinnerWithCoroutines()}") } println(" took $c ms on ${Thread.currentThread().name.substringBefore(" @")}") Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> val v = measureTimeMillis { println("blocking code on virtual threads: ${dinnerBlocking(vt)}") } println(" took $v ms") } val b = measureTimeMillis { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("blocking code on Dispatchers.IO: ${dinnerBlocking(Dispatchers.IO)}") } } println(" took $b ms") }

alt.title: ThreeWaysJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ThreeWays.kt: the same dinner with virtual threads (plain blocking code) // and with Reactor (operators, no blocking). Same total time: the slowest dish. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ThreeWaysJava { static String cook(String dish, long ms) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(ms); // a blocking call return dish; } static List<String> withVirtualThreads() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> soup = vt.submit(() -> cook("soup", 100)); Future<String> roast = vt.submit(() -> cook("roast", 300)); Future<String> salad = vt.submit(() -> cook("salad", 200)); return List.of(soup.get(), roast.get(), salad.get()); } } static List<String> withReactor() { return Mono.zip( Mono.just("soup").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), Mono.just("roast").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)), Mono.just("salad").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(200))) .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())) .block(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { withVirtualThreads(); withReactor(); // warm up long t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("virtual threads: " + withVirtualThreads()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("reactor: " + withReactor()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } }

try.expect: Every version takes about 300 ms: the coroutines, the blocking code on a virtual-thread dispatcher, the blocking code on Dispatchers.IO, the plain virtual threads and the Reactor Mono.zip. With withTimeout(250), the program fails with TimeoutCancellationException at about 250 ms, and the roast and the salad, still cooking, are cancelled with it. Doing that in the Java virtual-thread version would take extra code to cancel the futures yourself.

aside.title: What if my framework has already chosen?
aside.html: If you write web services, your framework probably has a switch for each model. Spring WebFlux runs on Reactor, and it also accepts Kotlin suspend functions as request handlers, converting at the edge for you. Quarkus can run a request handler on a virtual thread with its @RunOnVirtualThread annotation, and its reactive library, Mutiny, has Uni and Multi types that play the parts of Mono and Flux, with Kotlin coroutine bridges of its own. The rule of this section still holds: let the framework choose the model at the edge, and stay with it inside each part of your program.

compare.title: Three dishes for one table, with one deadline: virtual threads vs coroutines

java.title: Dinner.java
java.html: Dinner dinner(String table) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Soup> soup = vt.submit(() -> soupPot.serve(table)); // 1. three blocking calls, Future<Roast> roast = vt.submit(() -> oven.carve(table)); // one virtual thread each Future<Salad> salad = vt.submit(() -> salads.toss(table)); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(800); try { return new Dinner( // 2. one shared deadline soup.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), roast.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), salad.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException | ExecutionException e) { soup.cancel(true); roast.cancel(true); salad.cancel(true); // 3. cancel by hand throw e; } } // close() waits for every task }

kotlin.title: Dinner.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun dinner(table: String): Dinner = withTimeout(800) { // 2. one shared deadline coroutineScope { val soup = async { soupPot.serve(table) } // 1. three suspending calls, val roast = async { oven.carve(table) } // one coroutine each val salad = async { salads.toss(table) } Dinner(soup.await(), roast.await(), salad.await()) } // 3. a timeout or a failure cancels the other two automatically }

compare.note: Both take as long as the slowest dish, and both are cheap: a virtual thread or a coroutine per call. The difference is how much of the structure you write yourself. In Java with virtual threads, the calls can stay blocking, which is the big win, but the shared deadline, the step that cancels the other dishes on a failure, and the cleanup are your code. JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope covers that, but it is still a preview API (JEP 505). In Kotlin, the deadline is withTimeout, the other dishes are cancelled by coroutineScope, and the calls must suspend, or be wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher. Pick the model that matches the code you call: blocking libraries favour virtual threads, suspending ones and complex fan-out favour coroutines.

worked.title: Give the neighbour's Java program a door into the Kotlin kitchen

steps.say: The kitchen's real work is a Kotlin suspend function with retries: KitchenService.cook(order). The neighbour's Java program must call it from two places: a screen that works with futures and has a Cancel button, and a command-line tool that just waits for the answer. Neither can call the suspend function directly.
steps.code: class KitchenService(private val stove: Stove) { suspend fun cook(order: Order): Outcome = retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { stove.cook(order) } }

alt.html: // what the Java program sees: a Continuation parameter it can't sensibly supply public final class KitchenService { public final Object cook(Order order, Continuation<? super Outcome> $completion) { /* ... */ } }

steps.say: Add Java doors in a small Kotlin class with its own scope. One returns a future, for Java code that composes; one blocks with its own timeout, for callers that block anyway.
steps.code: class KitchenJavaApi(private val service: KitchenService) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) // 1. for Java code that composes futures fun cookAsync(order: Order): CompletableFuture<Outcome> = scope.future { service.cook(order) } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound fun cookBlocking(order: Order): Outcome = runBlocking { withTimeout(10.seconds) { service.cook(order) } } override fun close() = scope.cancel() }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same doors, if the service were a Java class returning futures final class KitchenJavaApi implements AutoCloseable { private final KitchenService service; KitchenJavaApi(KitchenService service) { this.service = service; } // 1. for Java code that composes futures CompletableFuture<Outcome> cookAsync(Order order) { return service.cookAsync(order); } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound Outcome cookBlocking(Order order) throws Exception { return service.cookAsync(order).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } @Override public void close() { } }

steps.say: The screen uses the future door, so its Cancel button can stop the Kotlin work: cancel(true) on the future cancels the coroutine, retries and all.
steps.code: // the screen is Java; this is the Kotlin side it relies on: cancel(true) reaches the coroutine val pending = api.cookAsync(order) pending.cancel(true) // 3. cancels the coroutine inside KitchenService, retries included

alt.html: // 3. the Java screen: show the outcome, or stop the kitchen when Cancel is pressed CompletableFuture<Outcome> pending = api.cookAsync(order); cancelButton.onClick(() -> pending.cancel(true)); // stops the Kotlin coroutine and its retries pending.thenAccept(outcome -> screen.show(order.dish() + ": " + outcome));

steps.say: A caller written with Reactor gets its own door from the same function, and the retry rules still live in one place.
steps.code: // 4. a cold Mono for Reactor callers fun cookMono(order: Order): Mono<Outcome> = mono { service.cook(order) }

alt.html: // 4. the Reactor caller's side Mono<Outcome> outcome = api.cookMono(order) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) .onErrorReturn(Outcome.REFUSED);

steps.say: Self-check: why not write cookAsync as CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { runBlocking { service.cook(order) } }? (It blocks a pool thread for every order, the future has no link to the coroutine so cancel(true) stops nothing, and the work belongs to no scope, so close() can't stop it either. That is the bug in this lesson's lab.)

lab.title: Three bridges between Kotlin and Java
steps: Meet the code. InteropModel.kt has an Order, the bakery's Java library (JavaBakery, which returns futures) and a Kotlin RecipeBook. KitchenDoor lets Java code call a Kotlin cook function, loavesLeftAwait lets Kotlin code wait for the bakery, and recipeMono hands a recipe to Reactor code. All three cross the fence with blocking calls. Run the tests: five of ten fail. One test, JavaCallerTest.java, is written in Java, to show what a Java caller of the door writes.
In KitchenDoor.kt, give the class a CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher), return scope.future { cook(order) } from cookAsync, and cancel the scope in close.
Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: future is an extension on CoroutineScope in kotlinx.coroutines.future. It is in the core library; no extra artifact is needed.
A coroutine cancelled through close() completes its future with a CancellationException, which is what a Java caller sees from get().
mono { } returns Mono<T> from a block that returns T?: a null completes the Mono empty, so the "no recipe" test needs no special case.
The tests on the starting code wait at most a few seconds each, so a stub never hangs the build. On the solution they finish in milliseconds.
lab.done: All ten tests in JavaInteropTest and JavaCallerTest pass.

drill.title: Three bridges from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class PantryDoor(private val pantry: Pantry) where Pantry has suspend fun stock(item: String): Int. Give it fun stockAsync(item: String): CompletableFuture<Int> for Java and fun stockMono(item: String): Mono<Int> for Reactor, both cancellable, and a close(). Then write suspend fun JavaButcher.cutAwait(order: String): Cut for a Java library whose cut(order) returns CompletableFuture<Cut>.

answer.html: class PantryDoor(private val pantry: Pantry) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) fun stockAsync(item: String): CompletableFuture<Int> = scope.future { pantry.stock(item) } fun stockMono(item: String): Mono<Int> = mono { pantry.stock(item) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } suspend fun JavaButcher.cutAwait(order: String): Cut = cut(order).await()

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: the Java and Reactor callers of those doors class PantryCaller { private final PantryDoor door; PantryCaller(PantryDoor door) { this.door = door; } int stockBlocking(String item) throws Exception { return door.stockAsync(item).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // blocks this thread: fine on a virtual thread } Mono<String> describe(String item) { return door.stockMono(item).map(n -> item + ": " + n + " left"); // cold, cancellable } }

recap: future.await() suspends on a CompletableFuture, unwraps its exception, and cancels the future if the coroutine is cancelled; asDeferred().await() waits without cancelling it.
scope.future { } gives Java a CompletableFuture for suspend code. Cancelling or completing the future cancels the coroutine, and closing the scope cancels everything still running.
mono { } is a cold Mono: one coroutine per subscriber, empty on null, cancelled on dispose. awaitSingle(), asFlow() and asFlux() cover the other directions.
Java can't call a suspend function in any useful way. Give it a future door, a Mono door, or a blocking runBlocking door with its own timeout, all wrapping one suspend function.

Virtual threads make blocking code cheap, coroutines add structure, cancellation and Flow, and Reactor gives operator pipelines with backpressure. Pick one model per part of the program, and convert at its edges.

The limit: a bridge carries a cancel only as far as the other side listens. A cancelled Java future may still finish its work, and a blocking call inside a coroutine ignores a cancel unless it can be interrupted.

explain.prompt: A friend is starting a new Java program that answers many requests at once. Each request makes three database queries through a blocking driver and calls one slow web service. Should it use virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor? Give your answer and the reasons.
explain.answer: I'd use virtual threads. The calls are blocking anyway and the code is Java, so one cheap virtual thread per request lets the team write plain blocking code with no rewrite, and on JDK 25 the old pinning problem with synchronized is mostly gone. I'd put a semaphore in front of the database and the slow web service, so the program can't overrun them. If parts of the program were in Kotlin and needed more than cheap blocking, such as several calls with one deadline, a cancel that reaches every child, or Flow pipelines, I'd use coroutines there, with the blocking calls on Dispatchers.IO or a virtual-thread dispatcher. Reactor would make sense only if a reactive stack already existed or we really streamed with backpressure end to end. Where models meet, I'd convert at the edge with future {}, await(), mono {} and awaitSingle(), which keep cancellation working, and never stack runBlocking and blocking get() calls in one call path.

deeper.html:
kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() is the supported route, and it gives every dispatch a fresh virtual thread. That makes it a good home for blocking calls inside coroutines, with two cautions. A coroutine blocked inside it still ignores cancellation unless the call is wrapped in runInterruptible, which interrupts the virtual thread. And the coroutine scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on one worker is lost, so code that relies on per-thread caches gets a new thread every time it resumes.

CompletionStage.await() works for any CompletionStage, not just CompletableFuture, and Deferred.asCompletableFuture() goes the other way for a coroutine you already started with async. On the Reactor side, Deferred.asMono() and Job.asMono() give hot Monos for work that is already running, and Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher() lets coroutines run on a Reactor scheduler, which keeps all the threads of a Reactor-based program in one place.

The structured-concurrency story differs most across the three. Coroutines enforce it by default. Virtual threads get it through StructuredTaskScope, a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505) whose shape changed between previews. Reactor has no tree of tasks at all, only operator chains that cancel upstream. When you bridge, the tree ends at the bridge: a future { } coroutine belongs to the door's scope, not to the Java caller, which is exactly why the door must own and close that scope.

Bridges and tests, the last lesson of the Kotlin Flow in depth track, comes back to callbackFlow and the Reactor bridges for whole streams.
